1	---
2	name: technical-excellence
3	description: >-
4	  Design and code standards for work that must stay correct: rich interfaces
5	  (errors, reason, invariants, parity tests), cited claims with grep-able ids,
6	  deep modules, a project lexicon with disciplined naming, type-level safety
7	  (invalid states unrepresentable, monoids, exhaustive matching), and a
8	  threat-model check on security. Use when designing an abstraction, writing or
9	  reviewing code or comments, naming things, or judging a review finding.
10	  Companions: test-quality (proving it), build-loop (the workflow).
11	---
12	
13	# technical-excellence
14	
15	Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.
16	
17	| Skill | Load it when |
18	|---|---|
19	| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
20	| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |
21	
22	First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
23	existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
24	is silent.
25	
26	## 1. Rich interfaces
27	
28	An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:
29	
30	| Part | Says |
31	|---|---|
32	| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
33	| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
34	| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
35	| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |
36	
37	**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
38	independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
39	only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.
40	
41	## 2. Claims are cited
42	
43	Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
44	claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
45	"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.
46	
47	Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):
48	
49	```
50	// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
51	...
52	// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
53	ack(token);
54	```
55	
56	- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
57	  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
58	- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
59	- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
60	  proof, and re-checks it.
61	- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
62	- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
63	  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.
64	
65	## 3. Deep modules
66	
67	Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
68	points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
69	forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
70	call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.
71	
72	## 4. Lexicon and naming
73	
74	Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
75	code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
76	do not use two words for one concept.
77	
78	Outside any convention:
79	
80	- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
81	- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
82	  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
83	- Be deliberate about grammar:
84	  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
85	    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
86	  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
87	  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
88	  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
89	- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
90	  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
91	  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.
92	
93	## 5. Type-level safety first
94	
95	Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
96	Reach for these before adding a check:
97	
98	| Tool | Effect |
99	|---|---|
100	| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
101	| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
102	| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
103	| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
104	| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
105	| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |
106	
107	If a runtime check or a test exists only to catch an invalid state a type
108	could forbid, change the type.
109	
110	## 6. Security stance review
111	
112	Security judgments are made against a **threat model**, never by reflex.
113	
114	1. Use the project's existing framework (a residual-risk framework, AGENTS.md
115	   invariants, an existing model).
116	2. If none exists, write a short `THREAT_MODEL.md`: assets, actors, trust
117	   boundaries, in scope, out of scope. Leave it UNCOMMITTED unless the user
118	   says otherwise.
119	3. Question the stance itself: which assets matter most, who can reach which
120	   boundary, what is knowingly accepted. Record accepted risks with a reason.
121	4. For each security-relevant change or review comment, decide: real exposure
122	   under the model, hardening nicety, or out of scope. State which and why.
123	5. Where a project limits reviewers to correctness findings, honor that for
124	   what you ask of them, but still assess security yourself.
125	
126	## 7. Judging review findings
127	
128	A finding is not a nit because it is small. Check it against: the claim it
129	contradicts (section 2), the invariant it breaks (section 1), the type that
130	could prevent it (section 5), and the threat model (section 6). Then apply
131	the smallest fix, with a test that fails without it (`test-quality`).
132

1	---
2	name: test-quality
3	description: >-
4	  What makes a test worth keeping, and the catalog of ways tests pass while
5	  proving nothing. Every test states its WHY (and CLAIM id); co-located tests;
6	  monoid laws, model-based state-machine properties, oracles, reviewed goldens,
7	  parity tests for mated interfaces; cheap manual mutation checks and periodic
8	  mutation tooling; explicit tautology hunting; plus the full failure-mode
9	  catalog with detection hints and fixes (tautology, over-mocking, asserting
10	  current behavior, happy-path only, host-timezone dependence, skipped
11	  fixtures, source-grep guards, wrong-layer pins, shared-table round trips).
12	  Use when writing tests, reviewing a test diff, fixing a red test, auditing a
13	  suite, or when a subagent (rg-implement or build-loop red phase) hands back
14	  tests. Companions: technical-excellence, build-loop.
15	---
16	
17	# Test quality
18	
19	A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
20	write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
21	red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.
22	
23	| Skill | Load it when |
24	|---|---|
25	| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
26	| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |
27	
28	## 1. Every test says why
29	
30	The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
31	short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.
32	
33	```
34	// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
35	//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
36	// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
37	```
38	
39	- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
40	  claim's grep finds its proof.
41	- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
42	  candidate.
43	- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).
44	
45	## 2. Placement
46	
47	Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
48	otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
49	is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
50	suites live apart, and say so in their why.
51	
52	## 3. Techniques worth using
53	
54	### Monoids and accumulators
55	If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:
56	
57	| Law | Property |
58	|---|---|
59	| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
60	| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
61	| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
62	| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |
63	
64	Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.
65	
66	### State machines
67	Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
68	transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
69	system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
70	transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.
71	
72	### Oracles
73	Expected values come from something independent of the code under test:
74	- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;
75	- a hand-computed fixture (arithmetic in a comment);
76	- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.
77	Beware a shared oracle: incremental-vs-forced parity can pass while both
78	paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
79	to the parity test.
80	
81	### Goldens
82	High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
83	the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained
84	(why: what it pins, version or pin it was generated at). Regeneration is a
85	deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.
86	Retain exact comparison for a fixed version; do not hide change behind a
87	blanket tolerance.
88	
89	### Parity tests for mated interfaces
90	Writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server: test both against literal
91	bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
92	against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
93	Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.
94	
95	## 4. Mutation checks
96	
97	**Cheap manual mutations (do these every time).** Pick 3-5 spots in the code
98	under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:
99	
100	| Mutation | If still green |
101	|---|---|
102	| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
103	| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |
104	| Change a constant (offset, threshold, default) | Value not asserted exactly |
105	| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |
106	
107	Use the result to decide: more tests needed, or tests that prove nothing
108	(remove them). Revert every mutation; never commit one.
109	
110	**`# catches:` and post-green spot mutations (build-loop red/green).** Each
111	red test carries a `# catches: <a plausible wrong implementation this fails>`
112	line. If you cannot name one, the test is likely a tautology; rewrite or drop
113	it. After green, the orchestrator applies 2-3 of those named wrong
114	implementations and checks the matching tests go red. A green implementer that
115	edits a red test says so in its report; the edit becomes a review finding.
116	
117	**Mutation tool, periodically.** If the stack has one (for example Stryker,
118	mutmut, cargo-mutants, PIT), run it every so often on a stable module.
119	Surviving mutants show gaps. Tests that kill no unique mutant and duplicate
120	another test's kills are candidates to prune, which keeps the standard suite
121	small and fast.
122	
123	## 5. Hunt tautology explicitly
124	
125	Before approving any test, ask of each assertion: *can this expression be
126	false given any implementation?* Tautology signs: value compared to itself;
127	mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test;
128	a literal's length asserted on the literal; a test of a pasted copy; a
129	mirrored formula. Mode 1 and 5 below, with fixes. For tautology, the
130	tool is the "revert the fix" mutation.
131	
132	## 6. The mutation check that catches most failure modes
133	
134	Mentally (or actually) mutate the code under test and see if the test fails:
135	
136	1. Revert the fix the test claims to pin. Still green? The test is wrong.
137	2. Delete the call site the test claims to cover (not the helper: the place
138	   production calls it). Still green? Wrong layer.
139	3. Empty the list, set or config the test iterates over. Still green? Vacuous.
140	4. Run it under `TZ=UTC` and under a DST zone. Different result, or a skip?
141	   Host-dependent.
142	5. Remove the fixture file. Skip with no CI failure? It never runs in CI.
143	
144	Before calling a suite done, do 1 for at least the tests whose names claim a
145	bug.
146	
147	## 7. Classic modes
148	
149	| # | Mode | Looks like | Fix |
150	|---|---|---|---|
151	| 1 | Tautology | Value compared to itself; mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test; `hasLength(12)` on a 12-item literal; `isNotNull` on a tear-off | Expected value from the spec or a hand calculation |
152	| 2 | Over-mocking | The engine/unit under test is stubbed; only fakes run | Mock the clock, network, platform. Never the unit |
153	| 3 | Asserts current behavior | Magic numbers with no derivation (`9.03`, `closeTo(50, 8)`); comment-free goldens | Show the arithmetic in a comment, or cite the spec/capture the value came from |
154	| 4 | Happy path only | No empty, null, zero, negative, NaN, boundary, duplicate, truncated, error, or thin-input case | List the edge cases before writing the first test |
155	| 5 | Mirrored implementation | Test re-implements the formula, or tests a pasted copy of a private helper | Hand-computed constants; test the real symbol |
156	| 6 | Coverage theater | Code runs, nothing meaningful is asserted; benchmark tests with no `expect` | Every test asserts a concrete value |
157	| 7 | Existence only | `isNotNull`, `isNotEmpty`, `returnsNormally`, `greaterThan(0)`, `isA<T>()`, `verify(called)` where the exact value is known | Assert the value. If the seeded row count is 3, assert 3 |
158	| 8 | Weakened during a fix | Exact value became a range; case deleted; `skip:` added; tolerance widened | Treat any loosened test in a fix diff as a red flag. Change the code, not the test. `git log -p` the test file |
159	| 9 | Volume over quality | Dozens of near-identical cases; parity corpora where the same records repeat (978 unique of 2,934) | Fewer, distinct cases; dedupe corpora and report the real count |
160	| 10 | Confidently wrong | Expected value contradicts the spec, docs, or the test's own earlier assertion | Flag uncertain inputs instead of guessing |
161	| 11 | Unreadable failure | `expect(cond, isTrue)` with no `reason:`; byte lists without hex | Match on the value, or add `reason:` naming expected vs actual |
162	| 12 | Blind golden | Snapshot regenerated by an env var; nobody inspected it | Golden only reviewed output; note who checked it and against what |
163	
164	## 8. Modes the classic list misses
165	
166	These came up across three repos, often in tests that looked careful.
167	
168	**Host-timezone dependence.** DST and local-vs-UTC tests that only bite when
169	the machine's zone differs from UTC, or that `markTestSkipped` unless
170	`TZ == America/Denver`. CI runners are UTC, so the check is vacuous there.
171	Calls that default to the host zone (no offset argument) also flip results
172	by zone. Fix: pin the zone inside the test, or pass the offset explicitly.
173	Never derive the expected value with the same `toLocal()` the code uses.
174	Run CI as a matrix: UTC plus one DST zone.
175	
176	**Silently skipped fixtures.** The test skips when a data file is absent,
177	and that file is gitignored or lives outside the repo. CI never runs it, yet
178	it's often the only end-to-end or real-capture test. Fix: commit a small
179	fixture, or make the skip loud in CI (fail when `CI` is set). Same for sibling
180	checkouts: a guard that skips unless `../analytics` exists, when the real
181	directory is `../openstrap-analytics`, has never run anywhere. Golden groups
182	that skip because the golden directory is absent are the same mode.
183	
184	**Source-grep guards.** "Ordering is untouched" checks that two identifiers
185	appear in a file; "prune order" checks `indexOf` positions; a "no 86400 s"
186	guard covers 22 hand-listed files and misses `86_400`. These pass if a comment
187	contains the string, if the code is reordered in a way the regex can't see,
188	or if the bug lands in an unlisted file. Fix: drive the behavior (seed a
189	partial day, prune, assert rows survive). Keep grep guards only as a backstop,
190	cover the whole tree, and include a positive control proving the pattern
191	matches something. A whole-tree scan for a new caller or forbidden dependency
192	is the legitimate kind (an audit of 88 guard files kept 18 of this type,
193	converted 48 to behavior tests, and removed 22).
194	
195	**Pins dead code or the wrong layer.** The test exercises a pure helper, but
196	production reads the value through a different path. Real examples: a
197	readiness-flash test pinning a getter with zero callers; a freeze test that
198	covers the pure function but not where the screen reads or the engine writes;
199	a race test that never imports the service and tests `List.remove`; an "edge
200	half" test that only calls the sibling library; "the stager only runs inside
201	`Isolate.run`" checked by two strings anywhere in the file (output parity is
202	not execution placement). Fix: test through the seam the user hits, or add a
203	test that the production path calls the helper.
204	
205	**Shared-table round trip.** The test builds a frame at offset 13 and the
206	parser reads offset 13 from the same constant. A wrong offset passes. Fix:
207	literal bytes from a real capture or the spec, decoded field by field. When a
208	real capture exists, assert every field you can hand-decode, not just the
209	version byte or the first 4 of 8 token bytes.
210	
211	**Capability tested once, wired N times.** The new decoder is tested
212	directly, but two other entry points still call the old one. Fix: count the
213	entry points and test each, or add a guard that they all route through one.
214	
215	**Iterating over the current set.** `for (op in dangerousCmds) expect(...)`
216	stays green when the set is emptied or an item is dropped. Fix: pin the
217	required members by name, then loop.
218	
219	**Conditional assertions.** `if (row != null) expect(...)` passes with nothing
220	checked. Fix: assert the precondition first.
221	
222	**Assertions on absence with no positive control.** "Nothing was written"
223	checked via `total_changes` or a log line, without proving the probe moves on
224	a real write. A no-bounce check that matches log wording passes if the log is
225	reworded. Fix: show the probe detects the positive case in the same test.
226	
227	**Test-only configuration.** The test runs with thresholds (300/200/200) that
228	differ from shipped defaults (200/150/750). Fix: test the shipped defaults,
229	plus overrides as separate cases.
230	
231	**Change-detector literals.** `expect(kAlgoVersion, 104)` or a literal SHA.
232	It fails on every bump and catches nothing. Fix: assert the property you care
233	about (the pinned commit contains the cited change).
234	
235	**Real time.** `DateTime.now()`, real `Future.delayed` sleeps, and "nothing
236	yet" checked after 300 ms. Flaky near midnight and on slow runners; a real
237	one-minute wait inside a correctness test costs a minute on every run. Fix:
238	`fakeAsync` with `withClock`, or inject the clock.
239	
240	**Tolerance that spans the plausible universe.** VO2max accepted in 30-70
241	when the hand value is 49.14; RMSSD up to 500 ms; one-sided bounds with no
242	upper limit; `closeTo(50, 8)` where the formula gives exactly 50 at z=0, so
243	weights and signs go untested. Fix: tolerance sized to numeric error, not to
244	"looks reasonable."
245	
246	## 9. Domain checks worth adding wherever they apply
247	
248	- **Absent input.** Missing or thin input returns null, absent, or "—", never
249	  a default or a value derived from another metric.
250	- **Idempotence.** Run the computation three times with slightly more data;
251	  the persisted value stays stable. Append a duplicate day; the baseline
252	  doesn't move.
253	- **Failure paths.** Every flag set on the happy path is cleared on error,
254	  timeout, and give-up.
255	- **Durability ordering.** Commit before acknowledge, tested by driving the
256	  real engine and observing the order, including a rollback case.
257	- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
258	  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.
259	
260	## 10. Grounding from suite audits
261	
262	Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
263	produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.
264	
265	| Lesson | What to do |
266	|---|---|
267	| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
268	| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
269	| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
270	| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
271	| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
272	| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
273	| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
274	| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
275	| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |
276	
277	## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)
278	
279	- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
280	  output. Show the arithmetic.
281	- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
282	- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
283	- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
284	- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
285	  say why in the commit message.
286	
287	## 12. When reviewing
288	
289	Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
290	catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
291	assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.

name: test-quality
description: >-
  What makes a test worth keeping, and the catalog of ways tests pass while
  proving nothing. Every test states its WHY (and CLAIM id); co-located tests;
  monoid laws, model-based state-machine properties, oracles, reviewed goldens,
  parity tests for mated interfaces; cheap manual mutation checks and periodic
  mutation tooling; explicit tautology hunting; plus the full failure-mode
  catalog with detection hints and fixes (tautology, over-mocking, asserting
  current behavior, happy-path only, host-timezone dependence, skipped
  fixtures, source-grep guards, wrong-layer pins, shared-table round trips).
  Use when writing tests, reviewing a test diff, fixing a red test, auditing a
  suite, or when a subagent (rg-implement or build-loop red phase) hands back
  tests. Companions: technical-excellence, build-loop.
---

# Test quality

A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |

## 1. Every test says why

The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.

```
// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
```

- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
  claim's grep finds its proof.
- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
  candidate.
- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).

## 2. Placement

Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
suites live apart, and say so in their why.

## 3. Techniques worth using

### Monoids and accumulators
If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:

| Law | Property |
|---|---|
| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |

Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.

### State machines
Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.

### Oracles

- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;

- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.

paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
to the parity test.

### Goldens
High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained

deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.

blanket tolerance.

bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.

under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:

|---|---|
| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |

| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |

- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.

## 10. Grounding from suite audits

Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.

| Lesson | What to do |
|---|---|
| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |

## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)

- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
  output. Show the arithmetic.
- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
  say why in the commit message.

## 12. When reviewing

Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.

---
name: writing-copy
description: Use when writing copy, meaning any text a person outside this session reads (docs, READMEs, UI strings, PR bodies, release notes, explainers, messages to the owner). Loads unslop and plain-writing and adds rules on eyebrow lines, why each piece of text exists, jargon, audience, compliance narration and a three-pass reread.
---

# Writing copy

Load `unslop` and `plain-writing` first, then apply these six rules.

1. **No eyebrow lines.** Omit the small label or kicker above a heading or
   title unless the request asks for one.
2. **Question every piece of text.** Name the question it answers and whether
   anyone is really asking it. People usually are not. Cut it if not.
3. **Keep jargon out of explainers.** One word per idea, defined once. Reuse
   that word; do not cycle synonyms.
4. **One named audience.** Know who reads it before you write, and write for
   that person.
5. **No compliance narration.** Do not explain how an action follows a rule
   or why it does not break one, unless the reader asked or the action really
   sits on the rule's boundary; then state the decision in one clause and stop.
   Never explain a distinction the reader set up or plainly knows. After a
   correction, report what changed; do not reassure in later messages. The
   test: what would the reader misread without this sentence? If nothing, cut
   it.
6. **Three passes before sending.** Reread the whole draft three times, each
   pass with one question: is every claim correct; does every sentence answer
   something the reader is asking; is any sentence about the writer rather
   than the reader's subject (self-justification, reassurance, credit, effort).
   Take the most care with that last kind: it is the easiest to miss in your
   own writing. Fix and reread after each pass.

Subagents load `unslop` and `plain-writing` only when they write copy, or when
a reviewer fixes comments (build-loop A7).

1	---
2	name: build-loop
3	description: >-
4	  Orchestrated red/green build with a scored cross-model review loop (Opus
5	  orchestrates, Sonnet and Sol implement, Sol or Opus review, Fable decides
6	  round 3) and triage of upstream review-bot comments. One working Claude
7	  agent at a time; reviewers have their own cap of one; only the owner raises
8	  it. Use for multi-phase features, or when the user says "build loop", "opus
9	  loop" or "sol loop". Companions: question-everything, technical-excellence,
10	  test-quality, vigil (manual-keepalive is the backup). After every
11	  compaction, reread this skill and vigil before anything else.
12	---
13	
14	# build-loop
15	
16	**After compaction: reread this skill.** A summary keeps the task but loses
17	these rules. When a session that used build-loop comes back from compaction,
18	reread this file, `vigil` and the reference for the step you are on before any other step. If work is in
19	flight, re-arm a vigil hold and start its background keepalive in that turn (§10). Compaction summaries preserve the reread and live-hold requirement.
20	
21	This file is a router; detail lives in `references/`. Section numbers are stable.
22	
23	**Load the companions.**
24	
25	| Skill | Load it when |
26	|---|---|
27	| `technical-excellence` | Before design or code, and when judging a finding. |
28	| `test-quality` | Before red, when tests come back, when a fix touches a test. |
29	| `question-everything` | Before a spec and before green (§4a). |
30	| `vigil` | As soon as work is in flight (§10); `manual-keepalive` only if vigil fails. |
31	| `qex`, `low-ram-hosts` | Before any heavy job (§8–9). |
32	
33	**Load the references at their step.**
34	
35	| File | Read it |
36	|---|---|
37	| `references/phases.md` | Before §3, before launching red, before green. |
38	| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
39	| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
40	| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
41	| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
42	| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
43	| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
44	| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
45	| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
46	| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |
47	
48	Scripts in `scripts/`: `review-ledger` (§6 ledger and briefs), `bot-triage`
49	(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
50	agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).
51	
52	## Dialogue before work advances
53	
54	Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
55	needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
56	Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
57	Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
58	disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
59	the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
60	work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
61	direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.
62	
63	Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
64	priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
65	`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
66	proposal approval.
67	
68	## 0. Boldness
69	
70	Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:
71	
72	> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.
73	
74	Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
75	skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
76	the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.
77	
78	**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
79	Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
80	something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
81	unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.
82	
83	## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)
84	
85	Do this first, in order:
86	
87	0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
88	   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
89	   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own branch and stays a reference; the
90	   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
91	   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
92	1. **Simpler alternative.** Does a simpler way exist (do less, reuse, change
93	   the requirement)?
94	2. **Desires.** Their first-order desire (what they asked for), second-order
95	   desire (why), and threat model (who can reach it, untrusted inputs, what it holds).
96	3. **Debate Socratically.** Question assumptions and offer counter-cases and
97	   cheaper options. Then write the agreed intent in 1-2 sentences: the review
98	   brief's Intent.
99	
100	Skip only for a fix whose intent is already unambiguous. If the user may be
101	away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a). Poorly scoped work: ask for
102	more detail first (`question-everything`).
103	
104	## 1a. Owner contact and decisions
105	
106	Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
107	AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).
108	
109	## 2. Roles and budget
110	
111	**Agent cap.** One working Claude agent (Opus, Sonnet, Fable, Haiku) at a time.
112	Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
113	raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
114	before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
115	writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
116	the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
117	are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
118	order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
119	advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
120	line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
121	runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
122	run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
123	are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
124	which run out faster now.
125	
126	| Role | Default | Does |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| Orchestrator | Opus (you) | Specs, prompts, verification, commits, pushes, owner contact. Writes little code. |
129	| Implementer | Sonnet and Sol, alternating by fix round (B1) | Red tests, green code, fixes. |
130	| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
131	| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
132	| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |
133	
134	B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
135	batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
136	the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.
137	
138	## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green
139	
140	Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
141	the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
142	batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
143	--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.
144	
145	## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)
146	
147	After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
148	bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
149	`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
150	`scripts/review-ledger`.
151	
152	Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.
153	
154	Rounds 1–2 use Sol or Opus, excluding authors. Round 3 uses Fable, then a
155	step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
156	stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.
157	The pilot schedule, score bars, checkpoint, cull and final-fix rules remain in
158	`references/review-v2.md`.
159	
160	Tier 2 is a fresh Opus pass, or Fable if Opus wrote code. After a passing
161	Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
162	schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
163	review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
164	`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
165	(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
166	smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
167	`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.
168	
169	## 7. Running Sol
170	
171	T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
172	substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.
173	
174	## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency
175	
176	On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
177	restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
178	jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
179	stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.
180	
181	## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct
182	
183	**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
184	to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
185	if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.
186	
187	**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
188	`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
189	start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
190	(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
191	pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
192	<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
193	releases, make a new hold in the same turn.
194	
195	"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
196	command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
197	(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.
198	
199	Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.
200	
201	## 11. Ship
202	
203	Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
204	loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
205	draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.
206	
207	## 12. Hand-off report
208	
209	Contents: `references/handoff.md`.
210

1	---
2	name: question-everything
3	description: >-
4	  Interrogate a feature before any implementation code exists, so defects are
5	  caught cheaply in the spec and red tests instead of in review rounds. Covers
6	  the designer interview (high-fidelity detail, push back), the questions to
7	  ask the user and yourself (which checklists apply, what is reusable, what
8	  recurs), turning recurring findings into project checklists early, and a
9	  bounded cross-model spec review (spec + red tests, up to two rounds) before
10	  green. Use at the start of any feature, before writing a spec, before the
11	  green phase, and whenever review findings start to repeat. Companions:
12	  build-loop (the workflow), technical-excellence, test-quality.
13	---
14	
15	# question-everything
16	
17	A defect costs least in a sentence of the spec, more in a red test, and most
18	in reviewed code. Spend questions early.
19	
20	| Skill | Load it when |
21	|---|---|
22	| `build-loop` | The feature is multi-phase; this skill is its pre-green gate (build-loop §4a). |
23	| `technical-excellence` | Shaping interfaces, invariants and types while you question the spec. |
24	| `test-quality` | Judging whether the red tests prove the spec. |
25	
26	## 1. Interview the designer
27	
28	The user is the designer. Get high-fidelity detail before anyone writes code.
29	Push back: an answer that leaves a state, edge or failure undefined is not an
30	answer yet.
31	
32	Ask, with a proposed default for each, so the user can answer in a word:
33	1. **States.** Every state the thing can be in, including empty, unknown,
34	   partial, stale, refused, failed. What does the user see in each?
35	2. **Edges.** Time (midnight, time zones, DST, nights that cross dates),
36	   units, limits, duplicates, retries, concurrency, offline, first run,
37	   upgrade from old data.
38	3. **Lifecycle of data.** Created, edited, deleted, exported, restored,
39	   merged, migrated: what happens to this feature's data on each path?
40	4. **Precedence.** When two sources disagree (user edit vs derived value,
41	   local vs backup, old vs new), which wins, and is that visible?
42	5. **Safety.** What must never happen (e.g. "never tell a wearer to skip a
43	   prescribed drug")? Write it as an invariant the types or tests enforce.
44	6. **Look.** Layout constraints the user cares about (stable row height,
45	   locked visuals). Get a mockup or golden description.
46	7. **Checklists.** "Which checklists should this run through?" Offer the
47	   project's existing ones as defaults (see §3).
48	8. **Reuse.** "What here could be reused elsewhere, or should reuse
49	   something that exists?" Offer your own candidates first.
50	
51	If the user is away, take the safe default, log it, and raise it later
52	(build-loop §1a). Never block.
53	
54	## 2. Ask yourself the same questions
55	
56	Before writing the spec, answer §1 yourself from the code:
57	- grep for existing seams that already solve part of it (a reconcile helper,
58	  a write seam, a scheduler, an id generator), and require their use;
59	- list every path the data travels (§1.3) and name the code for each;
60	- list the invariants and how each is enforced (type > test > review);
61	- list what is unknown, and how unknown stays unknown (never a silent zero).
62	
63	## 3. Turn recurrence into checklists, early
64	
65	Watch review findings across features. When the same family shows up twice
66	(e.g. "new table missing from export/restore", "delta arithmetic drifts from
67	the canonical total"), stop and write or extend a project checklist. Do not
68	wait for a fifth round. Keep checklists in the project (not in a generic
69	skill), each item citing the findings that taught it. Every later spec that
70	touches that area pastes the checklist, and the implementer answers each line
71	("done: <test>" or "n/a: <reason>").
72	
73	Also ask at each feature start: "Which recurring families could this
74	feature hit?" and pre-empt them in the spec.
75	
76	## 4. Cross-model spec review (before green)
77	
78	After the red phase commits and before any green code:
79	1. Send the reviewer (e.g. Sol) the spec, the red tests, the applicable
80	   checklists, and the designer's answers. Ask for: gaps (states, edges,
81	   lifecycle paths, precedence), contradictions, tests that would pass
82	   without the feature, missing invariants, and simpler designs or reuse.
83	2. Exchange at least one substantive argument with each spec reviewer before
84	   accepting its review, even an approval. Fable needs at least two. Give the
85	   reviewer the round priorities and invariants; record the exchange using
86	   build-loop `references/dialogue.md`. Fix the spec and red tests, then rerun the red gate.
87	3. At most two spec rounds. Anything still open after round two becomes an
88	   explicit decision (default + log + raise), not a third round.
89	4. Then implement, and run the normal code review loop (build-loop §6).
90	
91	The spec review is cheap: no code to read, so it should take one run.
92	Findings here save whole code-review rounds later.
93	
94	## 5. Signs you skipped this
95	
96	- review rounds keep finding new cases of the same family;
97	- fixes introduce ids, flags or columns the spec never mentioned;
98	- the implementer picks between designs mid-green ("I chose X over Y");
99	- defaults are discovered in reports instead of decided in the spec.
100	
101	When you see these, pause the loop and come back here.
102

1	---
2	name: technical-excellence
3	description: >-
4	  Design and code standards for work that must stay correct: rich interfaces
5	  (errors, reason, invariants, parity tests), cited claims with grep-able ids,
6	  deep modules, a project lexicon with disciplined naming, type-level safety
7	  (invalid states unrepresentable, monoids, exhaustive matching), and a
8	  threat-model check on security. Use when designing an abstraction, writing or
9	  reviewing code or comments, naming things, or judging a review finding.
10	  Companions: test-quality (proving it), build-loop (the workflow).
11	---
12	
13	# technical-excellence
14	
15	Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.
16	
17	| Skill | Load it when |
18	|---|---|
19	| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
20	| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |
21	
22	First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
23	existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
24	is silent.
25	
26	## 1. Rich interfaces
27	
28	An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:
29	
30	| Part | Says |
31	|---|---|
32	| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
33	| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
34	| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
35	| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |
36	
37	**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
38	independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
39	only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.
40	
41	## 2. Claims are cited
42	
43	Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
44	claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
45	"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.
46	
47	Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):
48	
49	```
50	// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
51	...
52	// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
53	ack(token);
54	```
55	
56	- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
57	  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
58	- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
59	- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
60	  proof, and re-checks it.
61	- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
62	- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
63	  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.
64	
65	## 3. Deep modules
66	
67	Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
68	points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
69	forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
70	call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.
71	
72	## 4. Lexicon and naming
73	
74	Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
75	code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
76	do not use two words for one concept.
77	
78	Outside any convention:
79	
80	- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
81	- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
82	  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
83	- Be deliberate about grammar:
84	  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
85	    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
86	  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
87	  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
88	  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
89	- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
90	  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
91	  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.
92	
93	## 5. Type-level safety first
94	
95	Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
96	Reach for these before adding a check:
97	
98	| Tool | Effect |
99	|---|---|
100	| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
101	| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
102	| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
103	| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
104	| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
105	| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |
106	
107	If a runtime check or a test exists only to catch an invalid state a type
108	could forbid, change the type.
109	
110	## 6. Security stance review
111	
112	Security judgments are made against a **threat model**, never by reflex.
113	
114	1. Use the project's existing framework (a residual-risk framework, AGENTS.md
115	   invariants, an existing model).
116	2. If none exists, write a short `THREAT_MODEL.md`: assets, actors, trust
117	   boundaries, in scope, out of scope. Leave it UNCOMMITTED unless the user
118	   says otherwise.
119	3. Question the stance itself: which assets matter most, who can reach which
120	   boundary, what is knowingly accepted. Record accepted risks with a reason.
121	4. For each security-relevant change or review comment, decide: real exposure
122	   under the model, hardening nicety, or out of scope. State which and why.
123	5. Where a project limits reviewers to correctness findings, honor that for
124	   what you ask of them, but still assess security yourself.
125	
126	## 7. Judging review findings
127	
128	A finding is not a nit because it is small. Check it against: the claim it
129	contradicts (section 2), the invariant it breaks (section 1), the type that
130	could prevent it (section 5), and the threat model (section 6). Then apply
131	the smallest fix, with a test that fails without it (`test-quality`).
132

1	---
2	name: test-quality
3	description: >-
4	  What makes a test worth keeping, and the catalog of ways tests pass while
5	  proving nothing. Every test states its WHY (and CLAIM id); co-located tests;
6	  monoid laws, model-based state-machine properties, oracles, reviewed goldens,
7	  parity tests for mated interfaces; cheap manual mutation checks and periodic
8	  mutation tooling; explicit tautology hunting; plus the full failure-mode
9	  catalog with detection hints and fixes (tautology, over-mocking, asserting
10	  current behavior, happy-path only, host-timezone dependence, skipped
11	  fixtures, source-grep guards, wrong-layer pins, shared-table round trips).
12	  Use when writing tests, reviewing a test diff, fixing a red test, auditing a
13	  suite, or when a subagent (rg-implement or build-loop red phase) hands back
14	  tests. Companions: technical-excellence, build-loop.
15	---
16	
17	# Test quality
18	
19	A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
20	write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
21	red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.
22	
23	| Skill | Load it when |
24	|---|---|
25	| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
26	| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |
27	
28	## 1. Every test says why
29	
30	The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
31	short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.
32	
33	```
34	// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
35	//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
36	// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
37	```
38	
39	- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
40	  claim's grep finds its proof.
41	- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
42	  candidate.
43	- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).
44	
45	## 2. Placement
46	
47	Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
48	otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
49	is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
50	suites live apart, and say so in their why.
51	
52	## 3. Techniques worth using
53	
54	### Monoids and accumulators
55	If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:
56	
57	| Law | Property |
58	|---|---|
59	| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
60	| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
61	| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
62	| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |
63	
64	Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.
65	
66	### State machines
67	Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
68	transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
69	system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
70	transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.
71	
72	### Oracles
73	Expected values come from something independent of the code under test:
74	- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;
75	- a hand-computed fixture (arithmetic in a comment);
76	- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.
77	Beware a shared oracle: incremental-vs-forced parity can pass while both
78	paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
79	to the parity test.
80	
81	### Goldens
82	High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
83	the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained
84	(why: what it pins, version or pin it was generated at). Regeneration is a
85	deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.
86	Retain exact comparison for a fixed version; do not hide change behind a
87	blanket tolerance.
88	
89	### Parity tests for mated interfaces
90	Writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server: test both against literal
91	bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
92	against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
93	Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.
94	
95	## 4. Mutation checks
96	
97	**Cheap manual mutations (do these every time).** Pick 3-5 spots in the code
98	under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:
99	
100	| Mutation | If still green |
101	|---|---|
102	| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
103	| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |
104	| Change a constant (offset, threshold, default) | Value not asserted exactly |
105	| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |
106	
107	Use the result to decide: more tests needed, or tests that prove nothing
108	(remove them). Revert every mutation; never commit one.
109	
110	**`# catches:` and post-green spot mutations (build-loop red/green).** Each
111	red test carries a `# catches: <a plausible wrong implementation this fails>`
112	line. If you cannot name one, the test is likely a tautology; rewrite or drop
113	it. After green, the orchestrator applies 2-3 of those named wrong
114	implementations and checks the matching tests go red. A green implementer that
115	edits a red test says so in its report; the edit becomes a review finding.
116	
117	**Mutation tool, periodically.** If the stack has one (for example Stryker,
118	mutmut, cargo-mutants, PIT), run it every so often on a stable module.
119	Surviving mutants show gaps. Tests that kill no unique mutant and duplicate
120	another test's kills are candidates to prune, which keeps the standard suite
121	small and fast.
122	
123	## 5. Hunt tautology explicitly
124	
125	Before approving any test, ask of each assertion: *can this expression be
126	false given any implementation?* Tautology signs: value compared to itself;
127	mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test;
128	a literal's length asserted on the literal; a test of a pasted copy; a
129	mirrored formula. Mode 1 and 5 below, with fixes. For tautology, the
130	tool is the "revert the fix" mutation.
131	
132	## 6. The mutation check that catches most failure modes
133	
134	Mentally (or actually) mutate the code under test and see if the test fails:
135	
136	1. Revert the fix the test claims to pin. Still green? The test is wrong.
137	2. Delete the call site the test claims to cover (not the helper: the place
138	   production calls it). Still green? Wrong layer.
139	3. Empty the list, set or config the test iterates over. Still green? Vacuous.
140	4. Run it under `TZ=UTC` and under a DST zone. Different result, or a skip?
141	   Host-dependent.
142	5. Remove the fixture file. Skip with no CI failure? It never runs in CI.
143	
144	Before calling a suite done, do 1 for at least the tests whose names claim a
145	bug.
146	
147	## 7. Classic modes
148	
149	| # | Mode | Looks like | Fix |
150	|---|---|---|---|
151	| 1 | Tautology | Value compared to itself; mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test; `hasLength(12)` on a 12-item literal; `isNotNull` on a tear-off | Expected value from the spec or a hand calculation |
152	| 2 | Over-mocking | The engine/unit under test is stubbed; only fakes run | Mock the clock, network, platform. Never the unit |
153	| 3 | Asserts current behavior | Magic numbers with no derivation (`9.03`, `closeTo(50, 8)`); comment-free goldens | Show the arithmetic in a comment, or cite the spec/capture the value came from |
154	| 4 | Happy path only | No empty, null, zero, negative, NaN, boundary, duplicate, truncated, error, or thin-input case | List the edge cases before writing the first test |
155	| 5 | Mirrored implementation | Test re-implements the formula, or tests a pasted copy of a private helper | Hand-computed constants; test the real symbol |
156	| 6 | Coverage theater | Code runs, nothing meaningful is asserted; benchmark tests with no `expect` | Every test asserts a concrete value |
157	| 7 | Existence only | `isNotNull`, `isNotEmpty`, `returnsNormally`, `greaterThan(0)`, `isA<T>()`, `verify(called)` where the exact value is known | Assert the value. If the seeded row count is 3, assert 3 |
158	| 8 | Weakened during a fix | Exact value became a range; case deleted; `skip:` added; tolerance widened | Treat any loosened test in a fix diff as a red flag. Change the code, not the test. `git log -p` the test file |
159	| 9 | Volume over quality | Dozens of near-identical cases; parity corpora where the same records repeat (978 unique of 2,934) | Fewer, distinct cases; dedupe corpora and report the real count |
160	| 10 | Confidently wrong | Expected value contradicts the spec, docs, or the test's own earlier assertion | Flag uncertain inputs instead of guessing |
161	| 11 | Unreadable failure | `expect(cond, isTrue)` with no `reason:`; byte lists without hex | Match on the value, or add `reason:` naming expected vs actual |
162	| 12 | Blind golden | Snapshot regenerated by an env var; nobody inspected it | Golden only reviewed output; note who checked it and against what |
163	
164	## 8. Modes the classic list misses
165	
166	These came up across three repos, often in tests that looked careful.
167	
168	**Host-timezone dependence.** DST and local-vs-UTC tests that only bite when
169	the machine's zone differs from UTC, or that `markTestSkipped` unless
170	`TZ == America/Denver`. CI runners are UTC, so the check is vacuous there.
171	Calls that default to the host zone (no offset argument) also flip results
172	by zone. Fix: pin the zone inside the test, or pass the offset explicitly.
173	Never derive the expected value with the same `toLocal()` the code uses.
174	Run CI as a matrix: UTC plus one DST zone.
175	
176	**Silently skipped fixtures.** The test skips when a data file is absent,
177	and that file is gitignored or lives outside the repo. CI never runs it, yet
178	it's often the only end-to-end or real-capture test. Fix: commit a small
179	fixture, or make the skip loud in CI (fail when `CI` is set). Same for sibling
180	checkouts: a guard that skips unless `../analytics` exists, when the real
181	directory is `../openstrap-analytics`, has never run anywhere. Golden groups
182	that skip because the golden directory is absent are the same mode.
183	
184	**Source-grep guards.** "Ordering is untouched" checks that two identifiers
185	appear in a file; "prune order" checks `indexOf` positions; a "no 86400 s"
186	guard covers 22 hand-listed files and misses `86_400`. These pass if a comment
187	contains the string, if the code is reordered in a way the regex can't see,
188	or if the bug lands in an unlisted file. Fix: drive the behavior (seed a
189	partial day, prune, assert rows survive). Keep grep guards only as a backstop,
190	cover the whole tree, and include a positive control proving the pattern
191	matches something. A whole-tree scan for a new caller or forbidden dependency
192	is the legitimate kind (an audit of 88 guard files kept 18 of this type,
193	converted 48 to behavior tests, and removed 22).
194	
195	**Pins dead code or the wrong layer.** The test exercises a pure helper, but
196	production reads the value through a different path. Real examples: a
197	readiness-flash test pinning a getter with zero callers; a freeze test that
198	covers the pure function but not where the screen reads or the engine writes;
199	a race test that never imports the service and tests `List.remove`; an "edge
200	half" test that only calls the sibling library; "the stager only runs inside
201	`Isolate.run`" checked by two strings anywhere in the file (output parity is
202	not execution placement). Fix: test through the seam the user hits, or add a
203	test that the production path calls the helper.
204	
205	**Shared-table round trip.** The test builds a frame at offset 13 and the
206	parser reads offset 13 from the same constant. A wrong offset passes. Fix:
207	literal bytes from a real capture or the spec, decoded field by field. When a
208	real capture exists, assert every field you can hand-decode, not just the
209	version byte or the first 4 of 8 token bytes.
210	
211	**Capability tested once, wired N times.** The new decoder is tested
212	directly, but two other entry points still call the old one. Fix: count the
213	entry points and test each, or add a guard that they all route through one.
214	
215	**Iterating over the current set.** `for (op in dangerousCmds) expect(...)`
216	stays green when the set is emptied or an item is dropped. Fix: pin the
217	required members by name, then loop.
218	
219	**Conditional assertions.** `if (row != null) expect(...)` passes with nothing
220	checked. Fix: assert the precondition first.
221	
222	**Assertions on absence with no positive control.** "Nothing was written"
223	checked via `total_changes` or a log line, without proving the probe moves on
224	a real write. A no-bounce check that matches log wording passes if the log is
225	reworded. Fix: show the probe detects the positive case in the same test.
226	
227	**Test-only configuration.** The test runs with thresholds (300/200/200) that
228	differ from shipped defaults (200/150/750). Fix: test the shipped defaults,
229	plus overrides as separate cases.
230	
231	**Change-detector literals.** `expect(kAlgoVersion, 104)` or a literal SHA.
232	It fails on every bump and catches nothing. Fix: assert the property you care
233	about (the pinned commit contains the cited change).
234	
235	**Real time.** `DateTime.now()`, real `Future.delayed` sleeps, and "nothing
236	yet" checked after 300 ms. Flaky near midnight and on slow runners; a real
237	one-minute wait inside a correctness test costs a minute on every run. Fix:
238	`fakeAsync` with `withClock`, or inject the clock.
239	
240	**Tolerance that spans the plausible universe.** VO2max accepted in 30-70
241	when the hand value is 49.14; RMSSD up to 500 ms; one-sided bounds with no
242	upper limit; `closeTo(50, 8)` where the formula gives exactly 50 at z=0, so
243	weights and signs go untested. Fix: tolerance sized to numeric error, not to
244	"looks reasonable."
245	
246	## 9. Domain checks worth adding wherever they apply
247	
248	- **Absent input.** Missing or thin input returns null, absent, or "—", never
249	  a default or a value derived from another metric.
250	- **Idempotence.** Run the computation three times with slightly more data;
251	  the persisted value stays stable. Append a duplicate day; the baseline
252	  doesn't move.
253	- **Failure paths.** Every flag set on the happy path is cleared on error,
254	  timeout, and give-up.
255	- **Durability ordering.** Commit before acknowledge, tested by driving the
256	  real engine and observing the order, including a rollback case.
257	- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
258	  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.
259	
260	## 10. Grounding from suite audits
261	
262	Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
263	produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.
264	
265	| Lesson | What to do |
266	|---|---|
267	| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
268	| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
269	| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
270	| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
271	| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
272	| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
273	| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
274	| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
275	| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |
276	
277	## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)
278	
279	- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
280	  output. Show the arithmetic.
281	- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
282	- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
283	- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
284	- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
285	  say why in the commit message.
286	
287	## 12. When reviewing
288	
289	Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
290	catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
291	assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.
292

5	
6	# Writing copy
7	
8	Load `unslop` and `plain-writing` first, then apply these six rules.
9	
10	1. **No eyebrow lines.** Omit the small label or kicker above a heading or
11	   title unless the request asks for one.
12	2. **Question every piece of text.** Name the question it answers and whether
13	   anyone is really asking it. People usually are not. Cut it if not.
14	3. **Keep jargon out of explainers.** One word per idea, defined once. Reuse
15	   that word; do not cycle synonyms.
16	4. **One named audience.** Know who reads it before you write, and write for
17	   that person.
18	5. **No compliance narration.** Do not explain how an action follows a rule
19	   or why it does not break one, unless the reader asked or the action really
20	   sits on the rule's boundary; then state the decision in one clause and stop.
21	   Never explain a distinction the reader set up or plainly knows. After a
22	   correction, report what changed; do not reassure in later messages. The
23	   test: what would the reader misread without this sentence? If nothing, cut
24	   it.
25	6. **Three passes before sending.** Reread the whole draft three times, each
26	   pass with one question: is every claim correct; does every sentence answer
27	   something the reader is asking; is any sentence about the writer rather
28	   than the reader's subject (self-justification, reassurance, credit, effort).
29	   Take the most care with that last kind: it is the easiest to miss in your
30	   own writing. Fix and reread after each pass.
31	
32	Subagents load `unslop` and `plain-writing` only when they write copy, or when
33	a reviewer fixes comments (build-loop A7).
